title: The Ramgarhia towers
hookLine: two tall towers built to guard the Harmandir still stand

lines: TWO BRICK TOWERS ABOVE THE ROOFS.
cards: Stand on the marble walkway around the pool at the Harmandir, look away from the golden shrine, and two brick towers rise above the rooftops near the edge of the complex. They don't glitter.
They look like what they were: lookouts. Sikh tradition says they belong to the bunga of Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, the carpenter's son this block met earlier.
Rest-houses once ringed the pool; this one still stands for people to point to.

teach.h: A TOWER LETS YOU SEE THEM COMING.
teach.b: A wall keeps people out; a tower lets you see them coming. In years when, as this path has told, armies came to Amritsar more than once, the people who loved the Harmandir needed early warning.

From a tower, a watchman could see the roads and fields beyond the city long before anyone at the pool. So the towers are about attention. Somebody climbs up, stays up and looks, while others below bathe, pray and sleep.

Guarding, in this picture, is mostly patience: hours of nothing, for the one moment that matters. Now notice who built them. Jassa Singh Ramgarhia came, tradition says, from a carpenter's family, a family of builders.
His band's gift to the Harmandir was not mainly gold. It was a building, made to protect someone else's prayers.
And notice the word still. Much of what stood round the pool in the misl years has been rebuilt or cleared, but these lookouts remain, and pilgrims walk past them to the shrine.

They've become a sign: a sacred place is something people have chosen to guard. The Harmandir sits low, at the level of the water, with doors open on every side; in Sikh telling, those doors are a welcome to all.
Just beyond that openness, someone built towers so the welcome could keep going.

how: Pilgrims at the Harmandir Sahib complex in Amritsar can see the towers of the Ramgarhia Bunga near the edge of the precinct, and Sikh histories remember Jassa Singh Ramgarhia as their builder.

games.q: you're a builder's son leading a misl. the Harmandir needs protecting. what do you give?
o: a chest of gold for the shrine.
towers to watch the roads from.
a new wall around the whole city.
games.why: tradition says Jassa Singh Ramgarhia's bunga rose into lookout towers, and they still stand.

practice: Bring to mind one precious thing that's easy to lose, a bedtime story, a friendship, a quiet morning hour, someone's trust, and take the watchman's post.
See what's coming down the road toward it, a busy month, a habit, a screen, and decide one small way to keep watch; if you pray, keep Waheguru on each breath out.
